title: Regime Change + Nation Building
description: The Islamic Republic collapses or is overthrown following decisive US military victory and a catastrophic humanitarian outcome that delegitimizes the regime domestically. This scenario represents the maximum US intervention footprint: regime change followed by a sustained nation-building enterprise analogous to Iraq post-2003. The preconditions are specific and demanding — a combination of near_collapse Iranian regime stability, decisive_us_victory resolution type, and catastrophic humanitarian cost — conditions that individually are low-probability but are correlated when a full-scale conflict exceeds 3 months with extensive ground operations or direct targeting of regime leadership infrastructure. The post-regime-change political landscape is shaped by three competing forces: (1) the Iranian diaspora, largely liberal and Western-oriented, seeking to establish democratic institutions with US backing; (2) ethnic and religious minorities (Kurds, Azeris, Baloch, Arab Khuzestani) seeking autonomy or independence in a power vacuum; and (3) reconstituted IRGC elements and hardline networks seeking to preserve institutional power under a new political shell. Iraq 2003 is the canonical reference — the US disbanded the Iraqi Army and de-Ba'athification in ways that destroyed governance capacity; the question is whether lessons were absorbed. The CBO estimated Iraq nation-building costs at $2–3 trillion over 20 years; Iran is 3x Iraq's population and 3x its geographic size, with significantly more sophisticated governance infrastructure that could either facilitate or resist reconstruction. Nation-building in Iran faces a unique dynamic: Iranian nationalism is exceptionally strong, including among reformists and anti-regime elements — the same populations who opposed the Islamic Republic would resist a perceived US occupation. The RAND Nation-Building study (2014) identifies 'host nation capacity' as the single strongest predictor of reconstruction success; Iran's pre-conflict technocratic and institutional capacity is substantially higher than Iraq's 2003 baseline, which is both an asset (capable governance partners exist) and a liability (those networks will resist US direction). The nuclear outcome in this scenario is the most ambiguous of the four: regime collapse creates a dangerous transitional period in which nuclear materials and scientific knowledge are both most vulnerable to non-state actor acquisition and most accessible for comprehensive verification — the 'loose nukes' risk and the 'full transparency' opportunity coexist. Reconstruction timeline assessment: 15–25 years to functional governance with sustained $50–100 billion/year US investment, based on Iraq and Afghanistan analogs scaled to Iranian population and territory.

title: Weakened but Intact Iran
description: The conflict ends with a negotiated settlement or declared US victory that leaves the Islamic Republic politically intact but strategically diminished — its nuclear program significantly set back, its conventional military degraded, its economic position worsened, and its regional proxy network weakened but not eliminated. This is the most analytically likely Phase 8 trajectory under the modal conflict scenarios: a short-to-medium duration conflict (weeks to 3 months) that achieves meaningful nuclear degradation without the domestic and international political costs of regime change. The Islamic Republic has survived severe stress before — the 8-year Iran-Iraq War killed 500,000 Iranians without toppling Khomeini; the 2009 Green Movement was suppressed despite mass mobilization; the 2019–2020 protests under crushing sanctions produced no regime transition. A 'weakened but intact' Iran is therefore the historically default outcome for even severe external shocks to the Islamic Republic's system. The post-conflict political equilibrium in this scenario features a regime that has absorbed the nationalist legitimacy boost from 'surviving' US military action (analogous to Saddam's domestic narrative after 1991), while conceding real strategic ground on the nuclear program under the settlement framework. The key long-term risk in this scenario is the regime's 'legitimacy debt' dynamic: having promised its population it would protect Iran and having failed to prevent US strikes, the regime faces pressure to demonstrate renewed strength — either through nuclear reconstitution, proxy activation, or diplomatic confrontation — within a 3–7 year window. RAND's conflict termination analysis identifies this as the 'wounded animal' dynamic: a regime that has survived external pressure but faces internal legitimacy questions is more likely to pursue confrontational policies than a fully secure or fully collapsed regime. The nuclear reconstitution timeline under this scenario — 4–8 years to breakout capability — means the conflict effectively delays rather than resolves the underlying nuclear crisis, setting the stage for a potential second round. The regional balance in this scenario is 'Saudi-Gulf ascendant': the conflict removes Iran as the primary regional security threat in the near-term, freeing Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Israel to consolidate their post-Abraham Accords alignment without the Iran threat overhang. Oil market recovery is substantial but leaves a $15–20/barrel risk premium that benefits Gulf state budgets.

title: Strategic Stalemate with Frozen Conflict
description: Active large-scale hostilities cease without a formal resolution, leaving the underlying political and nuclear disputes unresolved and the region in a condition of armed standoff. This scenario emerges from a specific convergence: the US achieves partial military objectives (degrading but not eliminating Iran's nuclear infrastructure), Iran retains enough asymmetric capability to make sustained US operations politically costly, and neither side can construct the domestic political coalition needed for a formal settlement. The 'frozen conflict' category in international relations literature — North Korea post-1953, Cyprus post-1974, Kashmir post-1998 — describes exactly this dynamic: active war ends, formal resolution does not occur, and the underlying conflict persists in a managed low-level state for decades. The specific mechanism for US-Iran freezing is: congressional war powers pressure forces a halt to offensive operations; Iran declares a unilateral 'strategic victory' in having survived; no ceasefire mechanism exists to formalize the pause; and both sides slip into a posture of 'armed truce' with periodic proxy escalations. This scenario is the most corrosive for long-term stability precisely because it combines the costs of conflict (infrastructure destruction, economic dislocation, political polarization) with the absence of conflict's resolutory benefits (negotiated constraints, diplomatic architecture, verification mechanisms). Iran's nuclear reconstitution is most rapid in this scenario: without a verification framework, the IAEA cannot operate in Iran, and the regime has maximum political incentive to rebuild nuclear capabilities as the primary deterrent against a repeat US strike. The 5-year nuclear reconstitution timeline in a frozen conflict scenario means that the US faces a renewed nuclear decision — strike again or accept a nuclear-threshold Iran — before the political wounds of the first conflict have healed. Regional actors adapt to the stalemate by hedging: Saudi Arabia and UAE simultaneously maintain US security relationships and expand Chinese economic ties; Turkey deepens its NATO-independent foreign policy; Israel maintains strike readiness while pursuing diplomatic normalization where possible. The frozen conflict is the scenario most likely to produce a 'multipolar fragmentation' regional order: the absence of a clear power-political resolution leaves a vacuum that multiple actors fill simultaneously, producing a more complex and less predictable regional environment than either a clear US victory or a clear settlement.

title: Regional Transformation
description: The conflict serves as a structural shock that transforms the Middle East regional order more comprehensively than any event since the 1979 Iranian Revolution — reshaping alliances, governance, economic architecture, and the regional security framework in ways that persist for decades. This scenario encompasses both positive and negative transformation pathways, unified by the common characteristic that the post-conflict region is qualitatively different from the pre-conflict baseline — not merely a return to a modified status quo. Positive transformation pathway: a decisive US military victory combined with an Iranian reformist resurgence and sustained US diplomatic investment produces a new regional security compact — an 'Arab-Israeli-Iranian' normalization framework analogous to the post-WWII European security architecture. Saudi-Iranian normalization deepens; the Abraham Accords expand to include other Arab states; and US-brokered multilateral security guarantees replace the informal deterrence system that preceded the conflict. RAND's 2023 regional security analysis identifies this as a 'best case' achievable only if the US sustains 15–20 years of diplomatic engagement equivalent to its post-WWII European investment — historically unprecedented for the Middle East. Negative transformation pathway: the conflict triggers 'catastrophic_regional_conflagration' with major involvement of Lebanon, Iraq, Yemen, and potentially Turkish and Gulf state forces. The collapse of multiple state structures simultaneously creates a power vacuum that no actor — US, China, or regional powers — can fill. The humanitarian catastrophe exceeds Syria in scale: 5–10 million displaced, multiple state failures, and a 20–30 year reconstruction horizon. Iranian nuclear material security in this scenario is the critical global risk: state failure + nuclear-capable scientific base + motivated non-state actors creates the conditions for nuclear terrorism that no international framework is designed to address. The 'regional transformation' scenario is analytically distinct because it captures the tail-risk, non-linear outcomes that dominate long-run assessments but are systematically underweighted by policymakers focused on base cases. CFR's 2024 global risk assessment identifies Middle East structural transformation — in either direction — as the highest-consequence low-probability geopolitical risk of the current decade.
